routes.label: Count occurrences and complete alphabet circuits

question:
A cryptographic code is designed as follows. The first time a letter appears in a given message it is replaced by the letter that is \(1\) place to its right in the alphabet (assuming that the letter A is one place to the right of the letter Z). The second time this same letter appears in the given message, it is replaced by the letter that is \(1+2\) places to the right, the third time it is replaced by the letter that is \(1+2+3\) places to the right, and so on. For example, with this code the word “banana” becomes “cbodqg”. What letter will replace the last letter s in the message

“Lee’s sis is a Mississippi miss, Chriss!”?
solution:
Only occurrences of the original letter \(s\) determine the replacement of the last \(s\). The words “Lee’s,” “sis,” “is,” “Mississippi,” “miss,” and “Chriss” contribute respectively
\[
1+2+1+4+2+2=12
\]
occurrences. The word “a” contributes none, so the last \(s\) is the twelfth occurrence.

Its shift is therefore \(1+2+\cdots+12\). Pair the first and last terms, then the second and next-to-last terms, and continue. There are six pairs, each with sum \(13\), giving
\[
1+2+\cdots+12=6\cdot13=78.
\]
Moving \(26\) places through the alphabet returns to the starting letter. Since \(78=3\cdot26\), this shift makes three complete circuits and returns to \(\boxed{s}\), choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
